children.translated_text: First, Section on Scriptural Testimony
Now, the <s>Gauḍapādīya-kārikāḥ</s> (verses composed by <s>Gauḍapāda</s>)
The outwardly cognizing, all-pervading is indeed <s>Viśva</s>,
the inwardly cognizing, however, is <s>Taijasa</s>,
the mass-of-cognition is likewise <s>Prājña</s>,
one alone, in three ways is (held; established) thus
At the right eye’s front is <s>Viśva</s>,
within the mind, however, is <s>Taijasa</s>,
in the <s>Ākāśa</s> (space) and in the heart is <s>Prājña</s>,
thus in the body he is disposed in three ways
For <s>Viśva</s> indeed enjoys the gross objects always,
<s>Taijasa</s> enjoys what is subtle and well-distinguished,
<s>Prājña</s> likewise is the enjoyer of bliss,
understand enjoyment as threefold
The gross satisfies <s>Viśva</s>,
the subtle, however, satisfies <s>Taijasa</s>,
and bliss likewise satisfies <s>Prājña</s>,
understand satisfaction as threefold
In the three abodes, whatever is the enjoyed object,
and whoever is proclaimed as the enjoyer,
he who knows this pair,
while enjoying is not tainted
The origination of all (beings) is,
for those who are real, the settled conclusion;
the <s>Prāṇa</s> gives birth to all,
the <s>Puruṣa</s> separately to rays of consciousness
Others, thinkers on creation,
consider it manifestation and production,
by others creation is imagined
as having the form of dream and <s>Māyā</s> (illusion)
“Creation is merely the Lord’s will,”
thus are some resolved regarding creation;
those who reflect on time consider
the birth of beings to be from <s>Kāla</s> (Time)
“Creation is for the sake of enjoyment,” say some,
and others say, “for the sake of play,”
this is the very nature of the god,
what longing could there be for one whose desires are fulfilled
As the remover of all sufferings,
the Lord, the master, the imperishable,
non-dual, of all entities,
the god, the fourth, the all-pervading, is remembered
Bound to effect-and-cause, those two,
<s>Viśva</s> and <s>Taijasa</s>, are admitted;
<s>Prājña</s>, however, is bound to the cause,
(the two; both) do not obtain in the fourth
Neither himself nor the other, indeed,
neither the true nor also the untrue,
<s>Prājña</s> is aware of anything,
the (fourth; <s>Turīya</s>) is always the all-seer

children.text: na satyaṃ na api ca an-ṛtam

children.translated_text: The non-grasping of duality is alike
for both, for <s>Prājña</s> and for <s>Turīya</s>;
<s>Prājña</s> is endowed with seed-like sleep,
and that is not present in the fourth
The first two are endowed with dream and sleep,
<s>Prājña</s>, however, with non-dream and sleeplessness;
neither sleep nor indeed dream,
do the knowers see in the fourth

children.text: na nidrāṃ na eva ca svapnaṃ

children.translated_text: Dream belongs to one who grasps otherwise,
sleep to one who does not know the truth;
when the confusion of those two is worn away,
he attains the state of the fourth
Asleep through beginningless <s>Māyā</s>,
when the living being awakens,
the unborn, sleepless, dreamless,
non-dual is then understood
If the world-process were to exist,
it would cease—there is no doubt;
this duality is mere <s>Māyā</s> (illusory appearance),
non-duality is in the highest truth
Thought-construction would cease,
if fabricated by anyone;
this doctrine is from instruction,
when known, duality does not exist
When asserting the identity of <s>Viśva</s>,
the commonalty of beginning is prominent,
upon the non-apprehension of the measure there would be
indeed only the commonalty of attainment
In the cognition of the identity of <s>Taijasa</s>,
eminence is seen clearly,
upon the non-apprehension of the measure there would be
a like twofoldness
In the presence of the <s>makāra</s>, for <s>Prājña</s>,
the commonalty of absorption is prominent,
but upon the non-apprehension of the measure,
there is only the commonalty of dissolution
He who, in the three abodes, whatever is alike,
knows the commonality decisively,
he is worthy of worship by all beings,
and is indeed the great sage to be saluted
The <s>akāra</s> leads to <s>Viśva</s>,
and the <s>ukāra</s> also to <s>Taijasa</s>,
and the <s>makāra</s> again to <s>Prājña</s>,
in name-only exists the progression
One should know the <s>Oṅkāra</s> by quarters,
the quarters are the measures—there is no doubt,
having known the <s>Oṅkāra</s> by quarters,
one should not think at all
One should yoke the mind to the <s>Praṇava</s> (<s>Oṃ</s>),
the <s>Praṇava</s> is the fearless <s>Brahman</s>,
for one ever united with the <s>Praṇava</s>,
fear exists nowhere
The <s>Praṇava</s> is indeed the lower <s>Brahman</s>,
and the <s>Praṇava</s> is remembered as the higher,
unpreceded, not internal, not external,
without another after, the <s>Praṇava</s> is imperishable
Of everything the <s>Praṇava</s> is indeed the beginning,
the middle, and also the end;
thus, having known the <s>Praṇava</s>,
one reaches That immediately thereafter
One should know the <s>Praṇava</s> as the Lord,
abiding in the heart of all,
having conceived the all-pervading <s>Oṅkāra</s>,
the steadfast one does not grieve
Measureless and having infinite measure,
the pacification of duality, the auspicious,
by whom the <s>Oṅkāra</s> is known,
he is a sage, not an ordinary person

children.text: iti (māṇḍūkyo1paniṣad-arthā3viṣ-karaṇa-parāyāṃ gauḍapādīya-kārikāyāṃ prathamam āgama-prakaraṇam [B:]gauda-pādīye āgama-śāstre āgamā3khyaṃ prathamaṃ prakaraṇaṃ samāptam)
children.translated_text: Thus (in the exposition that renders manifest the meaning of the <s>Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad</s>, in the <s>Gauḍapādīya Kārikā</s>), the first section, the <s>Āgama-prakaraṇa</s> (the section on scriptural testimony), is completed
Now, in the <s>Gauḍapādīya Kārikā</s>, the second section entitled <s>Vaitathya</s> (Falsity) begins
Second section <s>Vaitathya</s> (Falsity)
The falsity of all entities
in dream, the wise declare,
and the reason is the interior location of the entities
together with their being concealed (i.e., covered, not manifest)
And because of the brevity of time,
having gone to regions one does not see (them again);
and when awakened, indeed, every (entity)
does not exist in that place
And the nonexistence of chariots and the like
is heard, with proper reasoning;
therefore falsity is indeed arrived at,
they say, made evident in dream
But because of the interior location of distinctions,
therefore, it is remembered (to be so) in the waking state;
as it is there (in dream), so in dream again
it is not differentiated by concealment (i.e., by the factor of concealment)
For in the stations of dream and waking
the wise declare unity,
indeed by the very reason
of the equal status of distinctions (in both)
What is not at the beginning and at the end,
that is likewise so in the present;
being similar to what is false,
they are observed as though not-false

children.text: ādāv ante ca yan na asti

children.translated_text: The fact that they have purposes
in dream too is (also) admitted,
therefore, because they have a beginning and an end,
they are indeed remembered as false
There is (an) unprecedented state-bound property, indeed,
such as (belongs) to the dwellers in heaven;
having gone there, this one perceives them,
just as here a well-trained (man does)
But in the course of dream, the inner (object)
is imagined by the mind and is unreal,
while the outer is grasped by the mind and is real—
the falsity of these two has been seen
And in the course of waking too, the inner (object)
is imagined by the mind and is unreal,
while the outer is grasped by the mind and is real—
the falsity of these two is reasonable
If there is falsity of both,
of the two stations of distinctions,
who cognizes these distinctions,
who indeed is their maker of determinations (conceptualizer)
The Self by itself imagines the Self,
the Self, the Lord, by his own <s>māyā</s> (self-power of projection),
he himself cognizes the distinctions—
thus is the settled conclusion of <s>Vedānta</s>
He diversifies other entities
within, in the mind, (whether) unestablished or established,
and fixed ones too, outside, in the mind—
thus does the Sovereign imagine
And the time-factors that are within the mind,
and the twofold time-factors that are outside,
all these are merely imagined;
the differentiation has no other cause
And whatever are indistinct within,
and whatever are distinct outside,
all these are merely imagined;
the differentiation is due to the difference of the senses
He imagines the living being first,
then the variously characterized entities,
both external and internal indeed;
as is the knowledge, so is the memory
As a rope, not ascertained,
is imagined in darkness,
by forms such as a snake or a streak of water,
so is the Self imagined
When the rope is ascertained,
the imagining ceases;
‘it is a rope alone’—and thus non-duality,
so is the ascertainment of the Self
By <s>prāṇa</s> and the like, and by (indeed) endless entities,
by these forms it is imagined;
this is the <s>māyā</s> of that Lord
by which he himself is deluded
‘<s>Prāṇa</s>’—thus say the knowers of <s>prāṇa</s>,
‘elements (bhūtas)’—thus those who know that,
‘qualities (<s>guṇa</s>s)’—thus the knowers of <s>guṇa</s>,
‘principles (tattvas)’—thus too those who know that
‘feet (pādās)’—thus say the knowers of the ‘feet’,
‘objects (viṣayas)’—thus those who know that,
‘worlds (lokas)’—thus the knowers of worlds,
‘gods (devās)’—thus too those who know that
‘<s>Vedas</s>’—thus the knowers of the <s>Vedas</s>,
‘sacrifices (yajñas)’—thus too those who know that,
‘enjoyer (bhoktṛ)’—thus too the knowers of the enjoyer,
‘object of enjoyment (bhojya)’—thus too those who know that
‘subtle’—thus the knowers of the subtle,
‘gross’—thus too those who know that,
‘formed (with shape)’—thus the knowers of the formed,
‘formless’—thus too those who know that
‘time (kāla)’—thus the knowers of time,
‘direction (diś)’—thus too those who know that,
‘doctrines (vādas)’—thus the knowers of doctrines,
‘world-systems (bhuvanāni)’—thus those who know that
‘mind (manas)’—thus the knowers of mind,
‘intellect (buddhi)’—thus too those who know that,
‘mind-stuff (citta)’—thus the knowers of citta,
and ‘merit and demerit (dharma and adharma)’—thus those who know that
‘twenty-fivefold’—so say some,
‘twenty-sixfold’—and others,
‘thirty-onefold’—so they say,
and others (say) ‘infinite’
‘worlds’—the knowers of worlds declare,
‘stages of life (<s>āśrama</s>s)’—thus those who know that,
‘female, male, and neuter’—the gender-theorists,
and others (speak of) the superior and inferior
‘creation’—thus the knowers of creation,
‘dissolution’—thus too those who know that,
‘subsistence’—thus the knowers of subsistence,
and here, indeed, always (they say) all (this)
Whatever entity one might set forth to someone,

children.text: taṃ ca avati sa bhūtva āsau

children.translated_text: the mortal is not thus the immortal,
a change of <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) into something else
will never occur in any way
if that whose nature is immortal
in its own nature goes to mortality,
then, being made immortal by something contrived, for him
how could it remain unmoving
whether from what-is or from what-is-not, even so,
the teaching is the same when origination is posited:
what is determined and consonant with reasoning—
that is what stands, not the other
here, from the scripture’s ‘not this, not that (<s>neti neti</s>)’,
and ‘<s>Indra</s> by <s>māyā</s>s’, too,
‘unborn, yet manifold—’
he is said to be born by <s>māyā</s>

children.text: na iha nāna īti cā amnāyād

children.translated_text: and from the refutation of production,
origination is denied
‘Who indeed could beget him?’—thus,
the cause is denied
that very one—‘not this, not this’—
because he refutes what is explained,
since all, by the nature of being ungraspable,
is manifested as unborn by the reasoning

children.text: sa eṣa na iti na iti iti

children.translated_text: for the existent, birth through <s>māyā</s>
is admissible, but not in truth
in truth, for whom it is born,
what is born, indeed, is born of that
for the non-existent, birth through <s>māyā</s>
is by no means admissible in truth:
a barren woman’s son is not, in truth,
born even by <s>māyā</s>
as in dream the mind, by <s>māyā</s>,
trembles with the appearance of duality,
so, in waking, with the appearance of duality,
the mind trembles by <s>māyā</s>
and the mind in dream, non-dual yet with the appearance of duality—
there is no doubt
and so in waking, non-dual yet with the appearance of duality—
there is no doubt
this duality, whatever is moving or unmoving,
is a spectacle of the mind
for, when the mind reaches the state of non-mentation,
duality is not apprehended at all
when, by apprehending the reality of the Self,
he does not construct (mentally),
then he attains the state of ‘no-mind’,
through the absence of anything to be grasped
they declare knowledge to be non-constructive, unborn,
non-different from the knowable
<s>Brahman</s>, the knowable, unborn, eternal—
by the unborn it is awakened to the unborn
the movement of the mind
that is restrained, of the discerning one, without alternatives,
that indeed is to be understood,
different from deep sleep and not equal to it
for in deep sleep that (mind) dissolves,
the restrained (mind) does not dissolve
that very (state) is fearless <s>Brahman</s>,
the light of knowledge on all sides
unborn, sleepless, dreamless,
nameless, without form,
once-for-all manifest, omniscient—
there is no figurative predication whatsoever
beyond all speech,
beyond all thought,
supremely peaceful, once-for-all light,
samādhi—unshakable, fearless
there, there is no grasping nor releasing,
where thought does not exist
then knowledge, established in the Self,
has attained the evenness of non-birth
this is called the <s>asparśa-yoga</s> (the yoga of non-contact),
hard to behold by all yogins
yogins fear this indeed,
as seers of fear in the fearless
the fearlessness of all yogins
depends on the restraint of the mind:
the cessation of suffering and awakening, and
indeed the imperishable peace
just as the swelling of the ocean
by a single drop on the tip of a blade of grass,
so is the restraint of the mind—
it would be without exhaustion
by a method one should restrain
the distracted (mind) in the two—desire and enjoyment; and
even when very clear, in dissolution,
desire is like dissolution, likewise dissolution like desire
remembering all suffering,
let him turn away from the enjoyments of the body (or desire)
remembering the unborn-all,
he does not at all see what is born
in dissolution one should awaken the mind,
and when distracted, one should calm it again
if it is with latent impressions, let him discern; and
having reached equanimity, let him not disturb it
let him not taste the happiness there,
let him be detached, through wisdom
when the mind, unsteady, moves out,
let him gather it into one, with effort
when the mind neither dissolves
nor again is distracted,
without contact, without appearance—
then that is established as <s>Brahman</s>
self-abiding, peaceful, with nirvāṇa,
the inexpressible supreme happiness,
the unborn, by the unborn, as the knowable—
they describe as omniscient
no living being is ever born,
there is no origination of it
this indeed is the supreme truth:
where nothing whatsoever is born

children.text: iti (gauḍapādīya-kārikāyām a-dvaitā3khyaṃ [B:]gauḍapādīye āgama-śāstre '-dvaitā3khyaṃ) tṛtīyaṃ (prakaraṇam || oṃ tat sat || [B:]prakaraṇaṃ samāptam)
children.translated_text: thus, in the <s>Gauḍapādīya-kārikā</s>, the third chapter entitled ‘Non-duality’ is complete
now, the fourth chapter called ‘Quelling the Firebrand (<s>Alāta-śānti</s>)’
I bow to the best of bipeds,
who, by knowledge likened to space, (regarding) dharmas like the sky,
awakened to that which is non-different from the knowable,
has understood them
the <s>asparśa-yoga</s> (yoga of non-contact), indeed by name,
is beneficial for the happiness of all beings
undisputed and unopposed,
being taught—him I salute
some disputants indeed desire
the birth of what exists,
others, the wise, of what does not exist—
arguing with one another
Nothing that has become is born at all,
nor indeed is what has not become born
thus, disputing (whether dualistically or non-dually),
they in fact make known non-birth (<s>ajāti</s>)
The non-birth (<s>ajāti</s>) that is being made known by them,
we endorse
we do not dispute together with them—
learn the non-disputation
It is precisely the birth of the dharma that is unborn
that the debaters desire
for the dharma that is unborn is deathless (<s>amṛta</s>),
how will it come to mortality
The deathless does not become mortal,
nor conversely the mortal deathless
a change of <s>prakṛti</s> (intrinsic nature)
will in no way occur
If the dharma whose very nature is deathless
goes to mortality by its own nature,
then how will what is made deathless by something fabricated
stand firm as unmoving
What is accomplished-by-itself, innate,
(inborn, and) unmade—
that is to be understood as <s>prakṛti</s> (intrinsic nature),
which does not abandon its own <s>svabhāva</s> (self-nature)
All dharmas are, by their own nature,
free from old age and death
those who desire old age and death,
they fall away through that very conception
For whom the effect is the cause,
for him the cause is born
how can what is being born be unborn,
and how can that be permanent if different
If there is non-difference from the cause,
then the effect, for you, is unborn
but since the effect is indeed being born,
how will the cause for you be constant
For one for whom it is born from the unborn,
there truly is no example
and for one for whom what is being born is from what is born,
there ensues no fixed determination
For those whose beginning of the cause is the effect,
and the beginning of the effect is the cause,
the beginninglessness of cause and effect—
how is it to be set forth by them
For those whose beginning of the cause is the effect,
and the beginning of the effect is the cause,
thus birth would be for them
like the birth of a father from a son
If cause and effect occur,
then you must specify an order
for if they occur simultaneously,
there is non-connection, like a pair of horns
If, arising from the effect,
your cause does not become established,
how will an unestablished cause
produce an effect
If the ascertainment of the cause is from the effect,
and the ascertainment of the effect from the cause,
which is produced earlier,
upon whose ascertainment the other is dependent
Incapacity, non-cognition,
or disruption of sequence—
thus, in every way, by the wise,
non-birth (<s>ajāti</s>) has been made manifest
The example called seed-and-sprout
is always equal to what is to be proved,
but a cause that is equal to what is to be proved
is not appropriate in establishing what is to be proved
Non-cognition of before-and-after
is a clarifier of non-birth (<s>ajāti</s>)
for from a dharma that is being born,
how is the prior not grasped
Neither from itself nor from another,
does any entity whatsoever arise
whether existent, non-existent, or both existent-and-non-existent,
no entity whatsoever arises
The cause does not arise, being beginningless,
nor does the effect, by its own nature
for that of which there is no beginning,
there is no birth
Because conceptual imputation (<s>prajñapti</s>) has dependence on conditions,
and otherwise both would be destroyed,
and because of the apprehension of affliction,
a dependent existence (<s>paratantra</s>-existence) is held
That conceptual imputation (<s>prajñapti</s>) has dependence on conditions
is admitted from the seeing of reasoning,
that the condition has conditionlessness
is admitted from the seeing of what is real
The mind does not contact the object,
nor likewise its semblance as object
for since the object is unreal,
there is no semblance-of-object distinct from the object
The condition is not always mind
contacting in the three times,
how will misapprehension be without condition,
for that
Therefore mind is not born,
the mind’s object is not born
those who see its birth—
they indeed see the goal in the sky
Because it is from the unborn that (they say) the unborn is born,
therefore non-birth (<s>ajāti</s>) is the intrinsic nature,
a change of <s>prakṛti</s> (intrinsic nature)
will in no way occur
The having-an-end of what is beginningless—
for <s>saṃsāra</s> that will not be established,
and infinity for what has a beginning—
for liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) that will not be
What is not at the beginning and at the end,
that is likewise in the present
being like the unreal, though they exist,
they are designated as if not unreal

children.text: ādāv ante ca yan na asti

children.translated_text: Their having purpose,
even in a dream, is apprehended
therefore, because of having beginning and end,
they are indeed remembered as false
All dharmas are false in a dream,
as shown by the interior of the body
in that enclosed region,
whence is there sight of entities
To go and see is not appropriate,
because motion of time is not fixed
and all, when awakened,
are not present in that place
Having taken counsel together with friends and the like,
(having awakened [B:] having become fully awake) he does not attain (anything)
and whatever was grasped, even if it was something,
on becoming awake he does not see
And in a dream the body is without real substance,
since there is the seeing of another distinct from it
as the body is, so is everything,
a mind-seen, without real substance
Because of apprehension (grasping), as in waking,
that (same) cause is posited in a dream
and because (it) is the cause of that [B: and because of causality],
accordingly the waking is posited as conjoined with that
Because production is not established,
all is cited as unborn
nor, from what exists, of what does not exist
is there any arising whatsoever
Having seen the unreal in the waking state,
one who is of that nature sees it in a dream
and having seen the unreal even in a dream,
on awaking he does not see
There is no unreal that has an unreal cause,
nor likewise a real with an unreal cause
and there is no real with a real cause—
whence would the unreal with a real cause (arise)
Because of inversion (misapprehension), as in waking,
he might touch the unthinkable as if it were existent entities,
so too in a dream, because of inversion,
he sees dharmas right there
From apprehension and from customary practice,
for those who say that there is and that there is real-substantiality,
birth is taught by the Buddhas
for the sake of those who always tremble at non-birth (<s>ajāti</s>)
For those who tremble at non-birth (<s>ajāti</s>),
who fall away because of apprehension,
the faults of birth will not be established,
and even the fault (remaining) will be small
From apprehension and from customary practice,
as one speaks of a magical-elephant (<s>māyāhastin</s>)
from apprehension and from customary practice,
so one says: there is a real thing
A semblance of birth, a semblance of motion,
and likewise a semblance of thingness,
while non-birth, non-motion, and non-thingness,
are consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>)—peaceful, non-dual
Thus mind (<s>citta</s>) is not born,
thus dharmas are remembered as unborn
knowing exactly thus,
they do not fall into inversion
Just as the semblance of straight and crooked,
(the spinning of a firebrand [B:] the firebrand, made to spin),
so too the semblance of grasper and grasped,
(the vibration of consciousness [B:] consciousness, made to vibrate)
Just as a firebrand not spinning
is unappearing, unborn,
so too consciousness when not vibrating
is unappearing, unborn
When, indeed, the firebrand is spinning,
the appearances are not from elsewhere,
and when it is not spinning, they do not, from elsewhere,
enter into the firebrand
Nor have they gone out from the firebrand,
because there is no applicability of (its) being a substance
so too would it be in consciousness,
because of the non-difference of appearance
When, indeed, consciousness is vibrating,
the appearances are not from elsewhere,
and when it is not vibrating, they do not, from elsewhere,
enter into consciousness
Nor have they gone out from consciousness,
because there is no applicability of substantiality,
and because of the absence of effect–cause relation,
therefore they are always unthinkable
A substance would be the cause of a substance,
and indeed something other the cause of something other
but substantiality or otherness
for dharmas does not obtain
Thus dharmas are not born from mind,
nor indeed is mind born from dharmas
thus the wise enter
into the non-birth of cause-and-effect
As long as there is entry of cause-and-effect,
so long there is the arising of cause-and-effect
when the entry of cause-and-effect is exhausted,
there is no arising of cause-and-effect
As long as there is entry of cause-and-effect,
so long is <s>saṃsāra</s> extended
when the entry of cause-and-effect is exhausted,
(<s>saṃsāra</s> does not occur [B:] <s>saṃsāra</s> does not obtain)
By convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>) everything is born,
therefore the eternal is not
for by real nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) all is unborn,
therefore annihilation is not

children.text: śāśvataṃ (na asti tena [B:]tena na asti) vai

children.translated_text: Those dharmas which (are said) “to be born,”
(are born [B:] by convention), not in reality
their birth is like magic (<s>māyā</s>),
and that magic does not exist
Just as from a magical seed
a sprout of that same nature is born,
it is neither eternal nor subject to annihilation,
so the application in regard to dharmas

children.text: na asau nityo na ca ucchedī

children.translated_text: In all dharmas that are unborn,
the designation “eternal” or “non-eternal,”
where such categories do not apply,
discrimination is not spoken of there
Just as in a dream the mind (<s>citta</s>) moves,
by illusion (<s>māyā</s>), with a semblance of duality,
so too in waking, with a semblance of duality,
the mind moves by illusion
And the non-dual, with a semblance of duality,
is the mind in a dream—no doubt
and the non-dual, with a semblance of duality,
(likewise [B:] the mind) in waking—no doubt
While seeing a dream, moving about in a dream,
he sees living beings stationed in the ten directions,
whether born from eggs or from moisture,
those living beings whom he always sees
Those are seer-of-dream–mind-seen,
they do not exist apart from that
so too this, being seen by that,
is posited as the seer-of-dream–mind
Moving in waking, while awake,
he sees living beings stationed in the ten directions,
whether born from eggs or from moisture,
those living beings whom he always sees
They are to be beheld by the waking mind (<s>jāgrat-citta</s>),
they do not exist apart from that
Likewise, this is seen only as that seen of it,
it is accepted as the waking mind
For both, indeed, see each other as object and subject,
and one asks, “What is that which is?”
both are devoid of defining marks (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>),
they are apprehended only according to that doctrine

children.text: kiṃ tad asti iti ca ucyate

children.translated_text: Just as a dream-fashioned living being (<s>jīva</s>)
is born and also dies,
so these living beings, all of them,
both come to be and do not come to be
Just as a magic-fashioned (<s>māyā</s>-made) living being (<s>jīva</s>)
is born and also dies,
so these living beings, all of them,
both come to be and do not come to be
Just as an illusory construction (<s>nirmita</s>) of a living being (<s>jīva</s>)
is born and also dies,
so these living beings, all of them,
both come to be and do not come to be
No living being (<s>jīva</s>) is ever born,
its arising does not exist,
this is that highest truth,
where nothing whatsoever is born
This is nothing but the vibration of mind (<s>cittaspandita</s>),
dual, like the graspable and the grasper,
mind (<s>citta</s>) is eternally without an object,
therefore it is proclaimed to be unattached (<s>asaṅga</s>)
What exists by constructed convention (<s>kalpita-saṃvṛti</s>)
does not exist ultimately (<s>paramārtha</s>),
by dependent construction (<s>paratantra</s> abhisamvṛti) it may be said “it is,”
but not in ultimate reality
The unborn (<s>aja</s>) by constructed convention (<s>kalpita-saṃvṛti</s>)
is not even unborn in ultimate reality (<s>paramārtha</s>),
by dependent accomplishment (<s>paratantra</s> abhiniṣpatti) however, it is born by convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>)
There is clinging to what has not arisen (<s>abhūtābhiniveśa</s>),
duality is not present there,
having realized the absence of duality,
he is without conditions and is not born
When it does not obtain causes,
higher, lower, or middling,
then mind (<s>citta</s>) does not arise,
for, when causes are absent, whence the result
The non-sign-based (<s>animitta</s>) mind (<s>citta</s>)
has non-arising equal to non-duality,
for of what is altogether unborn,
that is indeed a mind-appearance (<s>citta-dṛśya</s>)
Having known the reality of signlessness (<s>animittatā</s>),
not obtaining any separate cause,
free from sorrow and likewise free from desire,
he attains the fearless state
Indeed, from clinging to what has not arisen (<s>abhūtābhiniveśa</s>)
it proceeds toward what resembles it,
having understood the absence of a real entity,
he, unattached, turns back
For one who has ceased and does not proceed,
then the abiding is indeed motionless,
that indeed is the domain of the Buddhas (<s>buddha</s>),
that unborn, equal, non-dual
The unborn, without sleep, without dream,
becomes dawn by itself,
for this indeed is once-for-all manifest,
a dharma whose nature is of the <s>dhātu</s> (elemental expanse)
Happiness is always veiled,
suffering is ever unveiled,
of whatever dharma whatsoever,
by grasping, that Blessed One (<s>Bhagavān</s>) is covered
“It is, it is not; it is, it is not,”
or again, “it is not, it is not,”
with the absences of both the moving and the stable,
the foolish one only covers over

children.text: asti na asty asti na asti iti
na asti na asti iti vā punaḥ

children.translated_text: These four groups of ten millions,
by whose graspings one is ever covered,
the Blessed One (<s>Bhagavān</s>) is untouched by these,
whoever sees him is an all-seer
Having attained complete omniscience,
the Brahman-status, the non-dual state,
without entering beginning, middle, or end,
what more beyond this would one desire
Indeed, this is the training of the <s>vipra</s> (the learned brahman),
quietude is called natural,
restraint, because of the pacification of nature,
thus the knower should resort to quietude
Both “with a real object” and “with apprehension”
are accepted as worldly duality,
both “without a real object” and “with apprehension”
are accepted as pure worldly
“Without a real object” and “without apprehension”
is remembered as supramundane,
the knower and the knowable should be known
as always proclaimed by the Buddhas (<s>buddha</s>)
And when, in the threefold knowledge and the knowable,
they are successively known by oneself,
omniprescience indeed, everywhere,
arises here for the great intellect
The objects to be abandoned, to be known, and to be realized,
are to be discerned according to the foremost vehicle (<s>agrayāna</s>),
apart from the knowable among them,
apprehension is said to be threefold
By nature like space, the knowables,
all dharmas are without beginning,
for there does not exist any diversity
of them anywhere whatsoever
Primordially awakened (<s>ādi-buddha</s>) by very nature,
all dharmas are well ascertained,
whoever has such forbearance (<s>kṣānti</s>)
is destined for immortality
Unarisen from the beginning to the end,
by very nature well at peace,
all dharmas are equally undivided,
the unborn equality, the mastery
But there is no mastery
for those who always roam in division,
sectarians sunk in differences,
therefore they are considered wretched
Wherever some will be
well ascertained in the unborn equality,
they indeed are great knowers in the world,
and that world does not fathom it
Regarding the unborn among the unborn,
knowledge of dharmas is to be accepted,
since knowledge does not proceed,
therefore it is proclaimed to be unattached (<s>asaṅga</s>)
When even a measure as small as an atom differs,
arising occurs for the undiscerning,
unattachment is never present,
how much less the falling away of coverings
All are those whose coverings have not been obtained
Dharmas are by nature stainless (<s>prakṛti-nirmala</s>),
in the beginning the <s>buddhas</s> likewise are liberated,
they are called leaders (<s>nāyaka</s>) because they awaken
For the <s>Buddha</s>, cognition (<s>jñāna</s>) does not proceed stepwise
into dharmas, O sufferer; [var.: O protector (<s>tāyin</s>)]
just so, all dharmas—and likewise knowledge—[are non-progressive],
this was not spoken by the <s>Buddha</s>
Hard to see, exceedingly profound,
the unborn equality (<s>aja-sāmya</s>), skillful and fearless,
having understood the state of non-manifoldness (<s>anānātva-pada</s>),
we pay homage according to our ability

children.text: iti (gauḍa-pādā3cārya-kṛtā māṇḍūkyo1paniṣad-kārikāḥ saṃpūrṇāḥ [B:]gauḍapādīye āgama-śāstre 'lāta-śānty-ākhyaṃ caturthaṃ prakaraṇaṃ samāptam)
children.translated_text: Thus the Māṇḍūkya Kārikās composed by <s>Gauḍapāda-ācārya</s> are completed; [var.: In the treatise of <s>Gauḍapāda</s>, the scripture of tradition (<s>āgama-śāstra</s>), the fourth chapter entitled ‘Cessation of the Firebrand’ (<s>Alāta-śānti</s>) is concluded]
